paper_name: Resource Hold Times under Multiprocessor Static-Priority Global Scheduling
paper_description: Studies computation of Resource Hold Times (RHT) for independently-developed real-time applications on multiprocessor platforms with clustered scheduling, where each application executes on a dedicated subset of processors using static-priority global scheduling and Priority Inheritance Protocol.

formal_description.statement: Resource Hold Time RHT_q_k_i is the maximum duration that task tau_i in application A_k can lock global resource R_q. RHT_q_k = max over tau_i in tau_q_k of {RHT_q_k_i}

variables.RHT_q_k_i: resource hold time of R_q by task tau_i in application A_k
variables.RHT_q_k: resource hold time of R_q by application A_k
variables.tau_q_k: set of tasks in A_k sharing resource R_q

assumptions: Tasks share global resources requiring mutual exclusion
formal_description.conclusion: Application's RHT is maximum among all tasks sharing the resource

informal_sketch.intuition: Resource hold time captures the longest duration any task in an application can lock a shared resource, important for bounding interference across applications.
steps: For each task tau_i accessing R_q, compute RHT_q_k_i
RHT_q_k_i includes: critical section length + interference from higher/equal priority tasks
Take maximum RHT_q_k_i across all tasks accessing R_q
Result is RHT_q_k for application A_k
key_insights: RHT abstracts resource requirements for independently-developed applications
Maximum over tasks ensures worst-case bound

formal_description.statement: Workload W_j(t, x) is maximum execution of x time units from task tau_j in interval t: W_j(t, x) = x * N_j(t, x) + min{x, t - x + D_j - T_j * N_j(t, x)}, where N_j(t, x) = floor((t - x + D_j) / T_j)

variables.W_j(t, x): workload of tau_j over interval t considering x execution units

formal_description.conclusion: Upper bounds total execution from tau_j emphasizing x-portion

informal_sketch.intuition: Workload calculation uses worst-case pattern where carry-in job executes late and subsequent jobs execute early, maximizing interference in the analysis window.
steps: Calculate N_j(t, x) = floor((t - x + D_j) / T_j)
Multiply N_j by x for full job contributions
Add min(x, t - x + D_j - T_j * N_j(t, x)) for carry-in job
Return total workload
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def compute_workload(tau_j, t, x):
    N_j = floor((t - x + tau_j.D) / tau_j.T)
    full_jobs = x * N_j
    carry_in = min(x, t - x + tau_j.D - tau_j.T * N_j)
    return full_jobs + carry_in
key_insights: Worst-case pattern maximizes specific execution portions

formal_description.statement: Response time RT_i under B-PIP equals: RT_i = E_i + DB_i + Ihp_dsr_i + Ihp_osr_i + Ihp_nsr_i + Ilp_i, where DB_i is direct blocking, Ihp terms are interference from higher priority tasks, and Ilp_i is interference from lower priority tasks with boosted priority.

variables.Ihp_dsr_i: interference from higher priority tasks on shared resources
variables.Ihp_osr_i: interference from higher priority tasks on other resources
variables.Ihp_nsr_i: interference from higher priority non-critical sections
variables.Ilp_i: interference from lower priority tasks with raised effective priority

formal_description.conclusion: Response time decomposes into execution plus multiple interference terms

informal_sketch.intuition: Response time includes base execution plus blocking/interference from both higher and lower priority tasks, where lower priority tasks can interfere via priority inheritance.
steps: Start with base execution time E_i
Add direct blocking DB_i from lower priority tasks
Add interference from higher priority tasks (three categories)
Add interference from lower priority tasks with boosted priority
Sum all terms to get response time bound
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def compute_response_time_BPIP(tau_i):
    RT = tau_i.E
    RT += compute_direct_blocking(tau_i)
    RT += compute_hp_interference_shared(tau_i)
    RT += compute_hp_interference_other(tau_i)
    RT += compute_hp_interference_noncritical(tau_i)
    RT += compute_lp_interference(tau_i)
    return RT
key_insights: Priority inheritance creates interference from lower priority tasks
Multiple interference categories must be accounted

formal_description.statement: Direct blocking DB_i = sum over R_q in R_A_k where tau_i in tau_q_k of n_i_q * max over rho_j < rho_i and tau_j in tau_q_k of {Cs_j_q}, where n_i_q is number of critical sections of tau_i accessing R_q.

variables.R_A_k: set of resources in application A_k
variables.tau_q_k: set of tasks sharing resource R_q
variables.n_i_q: number of critical sections where tau_i accesses R_q
variables.Cs_j_q: longest critical section of tau_j on R_q

assumptions: tau_i among m highest priority ready tasks
formal_description.conclusion: Direct blocking bounded by longest critical sections of lower priority tasks

informal_sketch.intuition: Direct blocking occurs when tau_i waits for a resource held by lower priority task; bounded by longest critical section per resource multiplied by access frequency.
steps: For each resource R_q that tau_i accesses
Find longest critical section among lower priority tasks on R_q
Multiply by n_i_q (number of tau_i accesses to R_q)
Sum across all resources tau_i uses
Return total direct blocking bound
key_insights: Only lower priority tasks can cause direct blocking

formal_description.statement: Under I-PIP, Ilp_prime_i = Ilp_i + sum over R_q in R_A_k where tau_i in tau_q_k and boost_q = rho_i of (max over rho_j < rho_i and tau_j in tau_q_k of {Cs_j_q}) / m

variables.Ilp_prime_i: interference from lower priority tasks under I-PIP
variables.Ilp_i: interference from lower priority tasks under B-PIP
variables.boost_q: boosted priority level for resource R_q

formal_description.conclusion: I-PIP adds interference from lower priority tasks with boosted priority equal to tau_i

informal_sketch.intuition: Under I-PIP, lower priority tasks immediately boost to resource ceiling, causing interference even when tau_i is highest priority task accessing that resource.
steps: Start with Ilp_i from B-PIP calculation
For each resource R_q where boost_q equals tau_i's priority
Find max critical section of lower priority tasks on R_q
Divide by m (parallel execution possible)
Add to Ilp_i to get Ilp_prime_i
key_insights: I-PIP causes more interference than B-PIP
Immediate priority boost affects highest priority task on resource

formal_description.statement: Assuming A_k is schedulable under PIP, there exists at least one boost level setting for global resources satisfying boost_q >= ceiling(R_q) for all R_q in R_G_k without making A_k unschedulable.

variables.boost_q: boosted priority level for global resource R_q
variables.ceiling(R_q): ceiling priority of R_q (highest priority of accessing tasks)
variables.R_G_k: set of global resources accessed by A_k

formal_description.conclusion: Minimum boost setting (boost_q = ceiling) preserves schedulability

informal_sketch.intuition: Setting boost levels to resource ceilings is equivalent to standard PIP, which preserves schedulability by assumption.
steps: Assume A_k is schedulable under PIP
Set boost_q = ceiling(R_q) for all global resources
This setting is identical to I-PIP semantics
Therefore schedulability is preserved
Higher boost values may or may not preserve schedulability
key_insights: Provides safe baseline for boost level optimization

formal_description.statement: Resource hold time RHT_q_k_i = Cs_i_q + Rh_q_i + Rl_q_i + Rb_q_i, where Cs_i_q is critical section length, Rh_q_i is interference from higher priority tasks, Rl_q_i is interference from lower priority tasks holding local resources, Rb_q_i is interference from tasks holding other global resources.

variables.RHT_q_k_i: resource hold time for R_q by tau_i in A_k
variables.Cs_i_q: critical section length of tau_i on R_q
variables.Rh_q_i: interference from higher priority tasks (priority >= boost_q)
variables.Rl_q_i: interference from lower priority tasks on local resources with high ceiling
variables.Rb_q_i: interference from lower priority tasks on global resources with high boost

assumptions: Task tau_i holds lock on R_q
formal_description.conclusion: RHT decomposes into critical section plus three interference categories

informal_sketch.intuition: While holding a global resource, a task can be delayed by higher priority tasks and by lower priority tasks with elevated effective priorities from other resource accesses.
steps: Start with base critical section length Cs_i_q
Add Rh_q_i: workload from higher/equal priority tasks divided by m
Add Rl_q_i: workload from lower priority tasks on local resources with ceiling >= boost_q, divided by m
Add Rb_q_i: workload from lower priority tasks on other global resources with boost >= boost_q, divided by m
Sum all terms to get RHT_q_k_i
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def compute_RHT_task(tau_i, R_q, boost_q, m):
    RHT = tau_i.Cs_q  # Critical section length
    RHT += compute_Rh(tau_i, R_q, boost_q, m)  # Higher priority
    RHT += compute_Rl(tau_i, R_q, boost_q, m)  # Local resources
    RHT += compute_Rb(tau_i, R_q, boost_q, m)  # Other global resources
    return RHT
key_insights: Three categories of interference during resource hold
Division by m accounts for parallel execution
Boost level determines which tasks interfere

formal_description.statement: Under multiprocessor global scheduling with PIP, there can exist multiple Pareto-optimal allocations of boost levels for global resources, where no boost level can be increased without decreasing another.

variables.boost_q: boosted priority level for resource R_q
variables.Pareto_optimal: allocation where no boost can be increased without compromising schedulability or decreasing another boost

formal_description.conclusion: Multiple incomparable optimal solutions exist, unlike uniprocessor case

informal_sketch.intuition: Unlike uniprocessors where single optimal boost allocation exists, multiprocessor interference interactions create multiple non-dominated solutions.
steps: For each possible boost level ordering, apply optimization algorithm
Different orderings yield different final boost allocations
Multiple allocations may be Pareto-optimal
No single allocation dominates all others
Multi-objective optimization techniques needed to find all Pareto solutions
key_insights: Multiprocessor scheduling creates complex boost dependencies
Order of boost optimization affects final allocation
